title: The stand at Chamkaur
hook: the Guru's elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, die fighting at Chamkaur, aged about eighteen and fourteen

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Anandpur, and a family scattered on the banks of the Sarsa. Your line was scattered, not lost. Did you reach someone far away? Day eighty-nine.

After the river, the Guru's group was tiny. Tradition says about forty Sikhs, and his two elder sons, Ajit Singh, about eighteen, and Jujhar Singh, about fourteen. They reached a village called Chamkaur, cold, wet and exhausted, and took shelter in a mud-walled house on high ground, more farmhouse than fort. By morning, the pursuing army had surrounded it. Tradition speaks of a vast force against forty. There was no way out. Today, the stand at Chamkaur, and two young men who walked out through the gate.
screen: `FORTY SIKHS AND TWO SONS.` → `A MUD-WALLED HOUSE.` → `SURROUNDED BY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Inside the walls, the Sikhs decided to go out in small groups of five, to hold the enemy back, knowing that those who went out would not come back. Tradition says the elder son, Ajit Singh, asked his father for permission to go. The Guru gave it, and helped arm him, and watched from the wall as his son fought and fell. Then the younger one, Jujhar Singh, about fourteen, came to him. Tradition says the Guru asked him if he was sure. He was. His father sent him out too, and he fell like his brother. Both of the Guru's elder sons died at Chamkaur, on the same day. Then something happened that shows what the Khalsa had become. The Sikhs left inside urged the Guru to escape, so that the community would not lose its Guru. He refused. So, tradition says, five of them, speaking as the Panj Pyare, as the Khalsa itself, gave him an order. And the Guru, who had knelt to receive amrit from five of his Sikhs, obeyed the five again. He slipped out in the night. One Sikh, Bhai Sangat Singh, who resembled him, put on the Guru's plumed turban and stayed behind so the enemy would think he was still inside. The Sikhs who stayed died at Chamkaur. Tradition says that among them was Kirpa Singh, the same man who, as Pandit Kirpa Ram, had come from Kashmir to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help. Two sons, and a handful of Sikhs, in a mud house. They stood.
screen: `OUT IN GROUPS OF FIVE.` · `AJIT SINGH, THEN JUJHAR SINGH.` · `THE FIVE ORDER THE GURU TO GO.` · `KIRPA SINGH, FROM KASHMIR.` · then, large: `THEY STOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit quietly for the elder sons. Settle, and breathe. Let the two names come softly: Ajit Singh. Jujhar Singh. About eighteen, and about fourteen. Think of someone you know at those ages, and let the story become real for a moment. You don't need to do anything with the feeling. Just sit with it, respectfully, the way people sit at a memorial. If you pray, you can pray in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Chamkaur. The village where Guru Gobind Singh's elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting, and the five ordered the Guru to live.
Your line: they stood. Today, when you feel outnumbered by something, a workload, a worry, a crowd, stand your ground for one more minute. Day eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Each December, Sikhs remember the battle of Chamkaur and the elder Sahibzade, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, with gatherings at Gurdwara Katalgarh Sahib and Gurdwara Garhi Sahib in Chamkaur.

fork.setup: you're the Guru. your sons have fallen, and five of your Sikhs, speaking as the Khalsa, order you to escape. what do you do?
options: refuse and stay to the end.
obey the five and slip out at night.
fork.reveal: the Guru obeyed the five, as he had knelt to them at Vaisakhi. Bhai Sangat Singh wore his turban and stayed behind.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Chamkaur, the village where the elder sons fell.

trapdoor: what you thought: a last stand in a battle.
what it means: two sons who stood, a handful of Sikhs who held, and a Guru who obeyed the Khalsa he had founded.
what a scholar hears: the Guru's own Zafarnama mentions forty men at Chamkaur; historians date the battle to December 1704 or 1705.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on the battle of Chamkaur and the deaths of Sahibzada Ajit Singh and Sahibzada Jujhar Singh
Zafarnama (Guru Gobind Singh's letter to Aurangzeb), on the forty at Chamkaur

notes: Ages about eighteen and fourteen follow the index; confirm.
The Zafarnama's reference to forty men (chihal) at Chamkaur is cited in paraphrase; confirm.

The order to leave given by five Sikhs (a gurmata) is tradition; some accounts name the Panj Pyare among them (Daya Singh, Dharam Singh, Man Singh left with the Guru; Himmat, Mohkam and Sahib Singh died at Chamkaur). Kept general; confirm.
Kirpa Singh (formerly Pandit Kirpa Ram) dying at Chamkaur is tradition; confirm.
Bhai Sangat Singh wearing the Guru's kalgi (plume) is tradition; confirm.
